title: 10 Animals With Superpowers That Sound Fake (But Are Real)
intro: Ten animals with abilities that sound like comic book powers. Every one is real and checked against a published study or a university, with the sources in the description. We start with a creature that survived being left outside in open space, and we finish with a shrimp that punches so hard the water around its fist boils. Let's go.

segments.heading: A tiny animal survived naked in outer space
segments.text: There is an animal that survived being left outside in open space, with no suit and no air. It's called a tardigrade, or water bear, and it's less than a millimetre long. In September 2007, a European mission called Foton-M3 carried about three thousand of them into orbit, 270 kilometres up, and opened the lid for ten days. Vacuum, freezing cold, cosmic radiation. When they came home, most of the ones shielded from the Sun's ultraviolet light simply woke up, walked off and laid eggs that hatched normally. Their trick is to dry out almost completely, swap the water in their cells for a sugar, and shut down. On Earth they have also survived temperatures near absolute zero. Eight legs, a tiny face, and tougher than any astronaut.

segments.heading: A frog that freezes solid and thaws back to life
segments.text: There is a frog that freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops. Its breathing stops. In spring it thaws out and hops away. It's the wood frog, and it lives as far north as Alaska. When the first frost comes, ice spreads through its body until up to two thirds of its water is frozen solid. Jon Costanzo's team at Miami University has kept Alaskan wood frogs frozen at minus sixteen degrees Celsius, others for twelve weeks, and watched them come back. The secret is sugar. The frog floods its cells with glucose, which works as antifreeze and keeps the insides of the cells liquid while the water around them turns to ice. When it warms up, the heart and brain thaw first, and within about ten hours the frog is back to normal. A gentle trick, compared to what the next animal does to water.

segments.heading: A shrimp that makes a bubble as hot as the Sun
segments.text: There is a shrimp that makes a bubble as hot as the surface of the Sun. It's the pistol shrimp, and it's about the length of your finger. One of its claws is oversized, and it slams shut so fast that a jet of water shoots out and rips open a bubble of near-empty space. When that bubble collapses, it makes a bang that is one of the loudest sounds in the ocean, with source levels of up to two hundred decibels. In 2001, a team led by Detlef Lohse at the University of Twente reported in Nature that the collapsing bubble also gives off a tiny flash of light, which means the inside reaches thousands of degrees, as hot as the Sun's surface for a split second. The shock stuns small fish, and the shrimp eats them. A finger-sized animal with a built-in gun.

segments.heading: A shark that was alive before the USA existed
segments.text: There is a shark swimming around right now that was probably alive before the United States existed. The Greenland shark lives in the freezing Arctic, grows about one centimetre a year, and takes about a century and a half just to reach adulthood. For years nobody could tell how old they got, because sharks have no bones to count rings in. Then, in 2016, Julius Nielsen and his team at the University of Copenhagen tried something clever. They radiocarbon dated the centre of the eye lens, which forms before the shark is born and never changes. The largest female they tested came out at roughly 392 years old, and even their cautious estimate put the lifespan at at least 272 years. That makes it the longest-living vertebrate ever found. It was already old when the first cars were built.

segments.heading: The salamander that regrows its own spinal cord
segments.text: There is a salamander that can regrow a lost leg, bones, muscles and nerves included, and it can repair a severed spinal cord too. It's the axolotl, a smiling pink amphibian from the lakes of Mexico that never really grows up. It keeps its feathery gills and its baby face for its whole life. Cut off a limb, and instead of a scar it grows a perfect new one. It can also regrow damaged tissue in the eye. In 2018, scientists in Vienna and Dresden finally sequenced its genome and published it in Nature. It is enormous: 32 billion letters, more than ten times the size of yours. Labs have kept axolotls for over 150 years, trying to learn how they do it. Because if we could copy even a fraction of this, a lost finger would just be an inconvenience.

segments.heading: A beetle that fires boiling chemicals from its rear
segments.text: There is a beetle that shoots boiling liquid out of its back end, and it fires like a machine gun. It's the bombardier beetle. Inside its abdomen it keeps two chemicals, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones, in one tank, and enzymes in another. When something grabs it, the beetle mixes them. The reaction is instant and violent. The spray comes out at about one hundred degrees Celsius, the boiling point of water, and it can aim it in almost any direction. In 2015, a team at MIT led by Christine Ortiz filmed living beetles with high-speed X-ray video and found the spray isn't one squirt. It comes in pulses, between 368 and 735 of them every second, which lets the chamber cool between blasts so the beetle doesn't cook itself. Ants that try it usually don't try twice.

segments.heading: An eel that delivers 860 volts
segments.text: There is a fish that can hit you with 860 volts, nearly four times what comes out of a wall socket in most of the world. In 2019, David de Santana from the Smithsonian and his team discovered that the electric eel of the Amazon is actually three different species, and one of them, named Electrophorus voltai, produced the strongest electric discharge ever measured from any animal. These eels grow more than eight feet long. They are not true eels at all, and most of that long body is packed with special cells that work like thousands of tiny batteries wired in a row. The shock stuns prey and sees off anything that tries to eat them. They have been living in the same rivers the whole time. We just hadn't noticed there were three of them.

segments.heading: A mammal that survives 18 minutes without oxygen
segments.text: There is a mammal that can go eighteen minutes with no oxygen at all, and walk it off. The naked mole rat lives in crowded underground colonies in East Africa, sometimes three hundred animals sharing the same stale air. In 2017, researchers including Thomas Park at the University of Illinois at Chicago put mole rats in a chamber with zero oxygen. They passed out after about thirty seconds, but their hearts kept beating, and after eighteen minutes they woke up fine. In air with only five percent oxygen, a level that would kill a mouse in minutes, they lived for five hours. The trick, published in Science, is that their bodies switch fuel. Instead of burning glucose, which needs oxygen, they run on fructose, the way plants do. Nobody had ever seen a mammal do that. Wrinkly, nearly blind, and built for the end of the world.

segments.heading: The platypus lays eggs, has venom and glows
segments.text: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, carries venom, hunts with electricity, and glows under ultraviolet light. Any one of those would be strange. The males have a venomous spur on each back leg. The females lay eggs, then feed the babies milk. Underwater, the platypus shuts its eyes, ears and nose completely, and finds food with its bill, which is packed with about forty thousand electric sensors that pick up the tiny pulses from a shrimp's muscles. And in 2020, Paula Anich and her colleagues at Northland College shone a black light on museum specimens and found the fur fluoresces a blue-green, which they published in the journal Mammalia. Nobody knows why yet. When the first specimen reached London in 1799, scientists thought it was a hoax. Honestly, fair.

segments.heading: The shrimp that punches so fast the water boils
segments.text: And the one we have been building up to. There is a shrimp whose punch is so fast that the water around its fist boils. The peacock mantis shrimp is about the size of your hand, and it keeps two club-shaped arms folded under its face. In 2004, Sheila Patek and her team at the University of California, Berkeley rented a camera that could shoot one hundred thousand frames a second. They clocked the strike at 23 metres per second, with an acceleration of up to eight thousand times gravity, and a force well over a hundred times the animal's body weight. The blow is so violent that bubbles of vacuum form on impact, and when they collapse they hit the victim a second time. Captive mantis shrimp have cracked aquarium glass. It eats crabs by smashing the shell off. Good thing it is small.

outro: So that's a frog that freezes solid, a shark older than the United States, and a shrimp that punches like a bullet. Which animal would you least want to meet in the wild? Tell me in the comments. There's a new fact here every evening.
description:
Ten animals with abilities that sound invented, from a tardigrade that survived open space and a frog that freezes solid every winter to a shrimp whose punch is so fast the water around it boils. Every fact is checked against a published study or university source; the links are below.
Which of these animals would you least want to meet?
